utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before we start this witness, I just want to raise this motion by the Prosecution filed on the 27th of March to tender documentary evidence, and a notification of an agreed fact. Mr. Bakrac, are you able to give us any sort of response to that so we can get it out of the way, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Good morning to all. The Defence has received the Prosecutor's motions and indeed everything that is mentioned in this motion is something that has been discussed by the Prosecution and the Defence, and we have agreed thereon. We have consulted our client as well, and the accused also does not wish to have the authenticity of the exhumation remains tested once again. If the families agree to that, we will not contest it. Also, we do not object having these exhibits put into evidence without bringing in an investigator or somebody else to testify. There is a reservation, though, with regard to Exhibits B and B1 if we understood it correctly, because the authenticity thereof has not been confirmed. The Defence and the accused, namely, believe that one word or two words, rather, added to his name were added subsequently by a person who is unknown to us, and that is the only reservation that the Defence has with regard to this. If the Prosecution agrees, we can enter this document into evidence without these additions, because it is obvious that the additions were made in a different handwriting. What was handwritten was handwritten in Cyrillic, whereas these words Commander of the Battalion have been written in the Roman script. Obviously somebody added this onto the document at a later stage, and that is the only objection the Defence has with regard to the authenticity of this document and with regard to our views concerning the entry into evidence of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You have no complaint about any of the other handwriting on that typed document; it's just those two words following your client's name at the top, in number 1 position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is what we challenge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, can you prove the authenticity of the two words that have been added to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We don't know when they were added and we do not know who added them and we do not dispute that it was not Mr. Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we will then have it noted that the documents -- that that document is admitted subject to the challenge which the Prosecution accepts to those two words; is that right? Do these have any identification numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then the document marked A will be Exhibit P445, and the one marked A1 will be P445/A. And the document which is presently marked B will be Exhibit P446 except for the words "Battalion Commander" written in handwriting beside the accused's name. And the document marked B1 will be Exhibit P446/1. I'm grateful to the parties for having agreed to those documents. Now, the business of the exhumations, the concession was stated in these terms: If the families do not object. Is it the fact that they have not objected to the reports going in?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't think that Mr. Bakrac meant that. The families had identified the bodies and, therefore, Mr. Bakrac does not object regarding the identification and doesn't want the family members to come here and tell us what they saw and how they recognised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think that's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I misunderstood him. Well, then, how do we deal with that one, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff? Have you got documents to be tendered or are we dealing again with Exhibit 55.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are dealing with Exhibit 55. The documents were already tendered and it's just the agreement that we do not call any more witnesses. It's not disputed that the bodies were of these two victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, now, we have a new witness. I'm sorry to have kept you waiting, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is still this business with Mr. Cancar, document C and D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes. Well, you want this to go into evidence in order to explain why you are not calling him; is that right? To stop any inferences being drawn against the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was discussed in the beginning when this trial started. We presented these documents and you actually advised to try to get the witness here and testify. But we were not able to do that. And it's just to prove that we made all efforts but unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, Mr. Bakrac, what do you say about the explanations in Exhibit C -- I'm sorry, the document C, D, and D1 going into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, such an explanation by the Prosecution is quite acceptable to the Defence, so we do not object to these reasons that have been put forth in terms of why Mr. Cancar cannot be brought in to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, then, Exhibit -- the document marked C will be Exhibit P447, and the document marked D will be 448. The document marked D1 will be 448/A. Thank you. Now, I'm told that there's a change in relation to the protective measures; is that so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness does not request any protective measures any longer. At first he did but now he wants to testify without protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, sir, would you please stand up and take the solemn declaration. Would you please make the solemn declaration in the document which is being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir, and I'm sorry that we've kept you waiting. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The 5th of December, 1950, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what is your name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Muhamed Lisica. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you also have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I have two nicknames. They called me Hamdo in my family, and people beyond my family called me Lija.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, although this witness has no protective measures, we have prepared a witness sheet for him, and it should be in front of the witness, with the names of other protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. That will be Exhibit P449 and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in front of you is a sheet of people with names of other protected witnesses, and I would like you to refer to their numbers when you want to refer to them and not name them by their names.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many children?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Two, a boy and a girl.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were born in Sarajevo. Where did you live before the war, immediately before the outbreak?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which part of Foca did you live?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Cohodar Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is it a Muslim neighbourhood or a mixed neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Cohodar Mahala is a big neighbourhood. In my immediate neighbourhood, 80 per cent of the population, approximately, were Serb, and 20 per cent was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What profession did you have before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Welder. A welder/mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I worked in Ozren. This was a service company called Ozren.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before the war, were you a member of any of the newly formed political parties?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I was not a member of any organisation as of three years prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And before these three years?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Before those three years, I was in the trade union, some kind of workers' council, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Immediately before the outbreak of the war, did members of your family leave Foca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: To Vojvodina. To Vojvodina. That's Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Should I give you a shorter version of this or should I tell you all about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: A shorter version, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: My brother was probably afraid of the war. He needed an alibi to go to stay with my family, or rather my wife's family, so he took my children to -- in order to bring my children to stay with their aunts and uncles there. He simply took them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why was your brother particularly afraid? Was there a reason?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I can't really say, but he was probably close to the Serbs to -- he went to restaurants and bars where the SDA and the SDS went out, and he probably heard lots of rumours. So I couldn't really tell you the exact truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was your brother in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: 70 per cent is the probability of his having been a member and 30 per cent is the probability of his having not been a member. But I did not look at his membership card.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. So you do not really know, but you think he was; is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't know. Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did -- and your wife, what about your wife? Did she also leave Foca?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that once again? She was in Foca. Oh, no. No. Well, she had worked too, and then she came home and then she phoned me and told me that my brother had taken my son and daughter to Vojvodina, and then she started to cry, and then I got her things ready for her so that she could go to Vojvodina on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It's a bit stupid to say this. I trusted the Serbs, that they wouldn't do anything to me, because I was friends with them all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you continue to work when --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly for how long, but I think I worked all the way up to the 6th of April, or perhaps it was the 5th of April. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Foca, did you participate in the fighting at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No, never. At no point.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the war started, where were you and where did you spend the first days of the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Partly in Foca, partly with my Serb neighbours. With Serbs, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you spend these days with Serbs and not at your house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Because I was alone at home. There was shooting. You'd get afraid a bit. I didn't know what to do. I sought their advice, so I stayed with them and then I'd go back home. I don't know. I can't really say. I was sort of terrified. How should I put it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon, you personally?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon in your house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. My bother, when he escaped, he left a rifle there and two or three grenades, something made out of dynamite. He left it there. I don't know how he got that rifle, but he left it there, so those weapons were in my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you do with the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You want me to give you the shorter version of that too or the longer version?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The shorter version first and if you -- you always give me the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shorter version first and if I need some additional details, I will ask you these additional details.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: All right. Milivoj Lucic took the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Lucic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: My neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he a soldier when he took the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He was in military uniform. He probably was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did he get the weapons? Did he know about the weapons, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, because I had been to his house before that, where there was a gathering of soldiers who were sitting there, and I wished them good luck. And they asked me to join their military and I said that I wouldn't join any army, not even my own, because this was not my war. And I told him that I had my brother's rifle, and he probably knew about it, and I said that it was at my place and then I said that they should not come to my house, that nobody should come to my house in the evening, and they said "Don't," and I might shoot if somebody would come or throw those grenades. They said, "No, do not shoot. Do not throw these grenades." So that's how it all happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Lucic actually take these weapons out of your house or did you give them to him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No. No. He didn't know how to find them. He searched the house, but he didn't manage to find them. And then he asked me and then I explained where it was and he personally took it and he put the rifle on his shoulder and he was carrying a plastic bag in his hands too, and well, I would say about 70 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Immediately after the outbreak of the war, did you observe the arrest of Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I don't know whether you could call it arrests, but they were taken to a house that was called Planika. It was below my house. Actually, this man worked in a Slovenian company, a shop that was called Planika and that's why he and his house were called Planika, so these people were taken to his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who took them to this house? Soldiers, the police, or --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Some wore civilian clothes, some wore military clothes. People were saying that they would take them there only for security purposes, safety purposes only, for a hearing or something like that. Some were returned home, women and children, whereas others remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you yourself ever taken to Planika's house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you tell us who took you there and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I cannot say who exactly took me, but I know how it happened. I ran out of cigarettes and then I went out of my house to a shop, to buy some cigarettes. Then some man, I don't know who it was. I think it was a man from Serbia proper. He pointed a gun at me, at my back, and he told me to walk ahead, and I told him that this hurt. Then he took me to Planika's house, and then I asked this same man to let me speak to his boss, right, his superior, and he said something like, "He's going to come here, and boy, will you be in trouble then." And then about an hour, an hour and a half later, a friend of mine, a former friend of mine, came. Now, just a second. Let me try to remember his name. Mitrasinovic, Goran. And he said hello to me and he asked me how I got there. I explained that I went out to get some cigarettes. And he gave me about a carton of cigarettes and he said to me that I should go back home. In the meantime the one who brought me said that he could take me back home, and he said, "He knows where he lives and he can go back on his own." And he said, "Well you know, don't get him out again." I can't give you his exact words, but that's the gist of it. That's the message.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrasinovic, was he the commander? You said this soldier was referring to a commander who would come. Was Mr. Mitrasinovic the commander?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, he had a belt, the kind of belt that was worn by officers and NCOs while I did my military service, and he also had a small bag which was usually carried by officers and NCOs before. So I imagine he was one of those who had some kind of authority or whatever. And he managed to release me. But what position he exactly had, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you what his position was or did he discuss what powers he had?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, yes. I don't know whether I can define it very precisely now, but he said -- I mean, this is a very long story. I have to give you a shorter version again. He said something like he knew who the good Muslims were, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know if other Muslim males had to stay in Planika house? Did you see others there who had to stay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, listen. Had to stay? I think they did have to stay there, because when I came to that house - I can't say exactly, but there must have been about 30 or 40 men there and the same number of women. The house was full. In front of that house there was a guard, and I entered the house and I did not manage to get out of the house until Goran Mitrasinovic got there. So most probably yes, they had to stay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were Muslims kept in other houses as well, other houses in your area? Did you observe anything like this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I know another house where I spent the night. That is the house that belonged to this man called Sandal. I don't know any others in Cohodar Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see -- from your house, could you see the Livade warehouses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. My house is sort of on that side and I usually sat on the balcony. And if there weren't lots of leaves in the trees, then I could see the warehouse and that side of the road completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see if Muslim civilians were kept there in the Livade warehouses? At that time we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I couldn't see that. I couldn't see whether they were holding Muslims there. I could see people walking about, but whether there were Muslims inside or not, that I could not see. You cannot distinguish between Serb and Muslim faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers using the warehouses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I saw men in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see civilians, and if so, what did they do there? What could you see?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I saw them walk up to the house only once. I was watching this from Mirko Kunarac's house through binoculars, because Mirko Kunarac asked me to see whether I knew someone. This was a group of people who were walking down the road toward this warehouse. There were soldiers in the front and soldiers in the back. They came to this warehouse and I stopped watching. So now, whether they entered this warehouse or not, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, I wonder if you could speak a little more slowly. You are making it difficult for the interpreters, who have having trouble keeping up with you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Fine. Great.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Sandal's house and that you spent a night there. When were you taken to Sandal's house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think I was taken away on the 17th of April, approximately sometime around 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who took you to Sandal's house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Goran Milicevic invited me from over there. He said, "Hamdo, come over." He said I should come there for some sort of interrogation. Then I asked him to give me some time, let me go and see my neighbour on some business. And he said, "Yes, go and see your neighbour, finish whatever you have to do and then come over."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Goran Milicevic, was he a soldier, a Serb soldier at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He was wearing a military uniform and he held a rifle in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see the neighbour that you spoke about, and who was he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Of course I did. That's my neighbour, a man I know very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was he, this neighbour? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: What do you mean, who was he?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The name. Can you give us the name of this neighbour?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The man I went to see or you mean Goran Mitrasinovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The man you went to see, who was this man?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: That is Mirko Kunarac, one of my good neighbours. In fact, I went to see Lekso Kunarac, but he was busy at the time and he said, "Go and see my brother." So I went to see his brother. I sat down and we had a chat and I asked him to tell me why I was wanted over there and what they wanted to do with me. Mirko Kunarac dialed a number. I don't know who he called.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you go to Lekso Kunarac and Mirko? Did they have a position that they could help you or why did you go to them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Because as a child, while I was living in Foca, they were friends of the family.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My question was, actually: Were they in a command position or did you simply go to them because they were friends?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Because we were friends, and in general, Mirko and Lekso Kunarac were influential people in Foca. They were no leaders by any means, but they had connections, they knew people that could help.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said Mirko called someone. Do you know who he called?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When he was making these telephone calls, were you present and could you hear what was said?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. I was there. He asked questions about me. He asked where is he going, what is going to become of him, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did Mirko tell you what was going to happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. He said I should go to this interrogation. He said I was going to the KP Dom and then I would spend 7 to 10 days there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you why you were supposed to be in the KP Dom for 7 to 10 days, why it was necessary?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Because it was general wisdom that Foca was going to fall, the Serbs were going to win, and there was not going to be a war at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was actually asking what Mr. Mirko told you. Did he tell you this, or what exactly did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He told me precisely what I've just told you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you when you would be released, on which this would depend?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that as well. You told me to give you a brief version and that's why I was trying to make it short. He said that probably Muslims would be divided into three groups. The first group would be the so-called honest people and then those who were guilty of something would be convicted. They would be divided into three groups: Honest people, less honest people, and completely dishonest people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you what would happen to the honest people in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He said they would be -- he said I would be released and I would go back to Ozren to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did he say about the not so honest people, the second group? What would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: They would be tried, they would be punished, some with a prison sentence, others would be put on probation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This third group that he mentioned, did he say anything what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He didn't say anything official, but I knew what he meant. It's a group of people who are no good, who should be killed or would be given 20 to 25-year prison sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is that what he said or is it what you simply thought?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, he said it and he didn't say it. He didn't say it in so many words, but he was telling a story from which I could gather as much. You know, you don't need to be told everything in so many words. If somebody tells you the first group will be spared, the second group will be punished, and the third group, he doesn't have to say what will happen to the third group. You don't imagine they will be spared as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived at Sandal's house, did you then actually go there on your own or were you escorted there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No. You see, Goran Mitrasinovic lives opposite Mirko Kunarac. It's like east and west. I went back and I reached this Milorad's house, and there was Goran Milicevic, who took me to his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We wouldn't need these details, actually. Did you go to Sandal's house alone or were you escorted there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I went halfway under escort and the other half I went on my own.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who escorted you? Soldiers or --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Goran. Goran escorted me, but he told me he was actually protecting me, since I was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mean you have mentioned two Gorans. You mean this Goran Milicevic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Milicevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived at Sandal's house, were there other persons already there, civilians, I mean?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, there were Muslims, women and men.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Sandal's house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: From 12.00 until the next day at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you interrogated at that house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who interrogated you, and what were you asked?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I was interrogated by Vajo Kunarac. He was actually present. They asked me what kind of weapons I had. That's all, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you eventually taken to the KP Dom then, the next day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you taken alone or in a group of people?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The women were released, and men were put on a bus. Those were in fact people from Serbia proper. I don't know whether they were eagles or not, but they put us in a bus. And if you could put 50 people on a bus, there were 10 more standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those on the bus, were they all Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that there were people from Serbia proper there. Do you mean soldiers who escorted you to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned the bus. Was it a military bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No. It was a bus belonging to the Maglic company. That's a work organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the driver of the bus, was he also a soldier or was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I cannot tell you for sure. I know who was driving, but I wouldn't be able to tell you what kind of uniform he was wearing, if any, because I got into the bus through the back door.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you arrive at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: That could have been the 18th of April, between 1.00 and 3.00; in fact, around 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: In October 1994 I was released. I cannot remember the exact date, but everybody knows when we left. I think it was in October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, who received you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Soldiers from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see any regular guards at the KP Dom at that day when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think that when I arrived, if I remember correctly, not a single Serb from Foca was there. Everyone there were Serbian soldiers from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you mistreated or abused on your arrival?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: They did mistreat us, but you would have to explain to me what you mean by "abuse."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did they do to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: They cursed us, they attacked us verbally, provoked us, in a political sense, saying things like, "See what Alija has done to you." Then they made us file into the KP Dom and I went into Room 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, were you searched?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Before I got into the KP Dom I was searched.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you registered? Were your particulars taken down on your arrival?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: When we came into the room, I found there a group of people who had already come on the 17th from a place called Livade. There was a man there nicknamed Uco, which means a teacher, and they came and took down our personal details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This Uco, was he one of the Serb soldiers or was he a detainee?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: That was a Serb soldier who didn't carry any weapons. He was wearing a uniform. A Serb soldier from Serbia, the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said, "They took down our personal details." How much of your details? Just the name or the profession, the birth date? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned personally, I was asked my name and surname. I told them, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to Room 11. Where was it within the building? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, it was in the KP Dom of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but can you describe in which building it was, I mean, in which of the prisoners' buildings and on which floor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: When you come into the KP Dom, then it's on the left-hand side, on the ground floor. The left building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Room 11, approximately? Not the date, of course.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly. I can tell you only roughly, because I've been in many rooms. It was maybe two months, maybe three. I really don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall to which room you were taken next after Room 11?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think I was once in a room where Alija Izetbegovic had been because I saw his particulars there. I think it's Room 17. I'm saying about Alija to make it more easily understandable for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I would like to show the witness photograph 7512 of Exhibit 18. That's this photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you -- you have to point it out --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think this room here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have to point it out on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: This floor. I think -- in fact, I'm afraid I couldn't tell you exactly. It's one of these two. I think it's more probably this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing first at the first floor and then at the second floor. That would be either Room 18 or Room 20, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said you were transferred to several other rooms. Have you ever been on the top floor of this building which is marked with a number 2 on this photo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I was in Room 22. I think -- you are confusing me a little, because I spent time in those rooms. I didn't look at the numbers. I think they are located here somewhere. I don't know what the number is. This is 18 and this is 22. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we have a look at the lower photo? Can you please move the photo so that we can look at this -- this is the photo 7513. Witness, you were pointing at windows where you -- of a room on the top floor. Here you have it a little bit better. Can you point out in which room you were when you were on the top floor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I was up here where these windows are. I wouldn't know what room this is. I think it's 22. And that one is 23. I think that was Room 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing at the building marked with a 3, and he was pointing at the left windows of the top floor. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From this room, could you see the bridge over the Drina in front of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I didn't look much through that window. I think you can see the bridge, but only the upper part, the arch of the bridge. I wouldn't dare claim anything with any certainty. I didn't look much through that window. I didn't look over to the other side. I think you can see across the bridge, but whether you can really see what's under the bridge, like the cars going underneath, I'm not sure. You could see across the bridge and the road across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Has there been any resolution about this problem with the photographs yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Defence counsel had actually provided photos that they made from the top floor, but I thought that they would point it to the witness. I actually wanted to use our photos because we have not yet any markings on the photos. But I can, of course, do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter for you. The strict way in which this should have been done, if we had had access to the KP Dom more easily, would have been for the Prosecution to show a photograph if they relied upon it, for the Defence to show if they relied upon it. Now that you've got the photograph, are you able to identify from which windows they were taken?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you are in great difficulty, then. Perhaps you had better waited for the Defence to use it. It's unfortunate, because we're now running out of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness the below-up version of the photo 7528. It's a Prosecution photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would that be the view that you had from this room where you were in on the top floor? Could you say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can say that. You could see this from the window -- because I remember I was looking at this house. This could be it, because this is precisely the arch you can see that I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He showed the -- he showed whatever it is marked with the arrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, as I do not know if the Defence counsel will use their photos with this witness, I would need to use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think we can say quite safely that if the Defence don't use their photographs, then the inference will be available that they don't use them because they don't assist their case, now that we know that they've got them. What's the situation, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to apologise first of all. We wanted to make the identification together with all the other evidence and then present it when we have all the evidence completed. But we were not able to use these photographs, because this witness had not mentioned in his earlier statements that he had been in the upper floor. However, since we now have this photograph presented by the Prosecution, and he confirmed that he had been there, and we agreed, moreover, that it is Room 22 indeed, then there is no need to present him with our photographs, because he pointed to the room exactly and he said that was the view from the room. So I don't think there is any need for us to show anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But I think that I should make it clear, Mr. Bakrac, that the inference which I personally would draw from that statement is that your photographs taken from that top floor and Room 22, do not suggest that you cannot see at least the top of the arch of the bridge; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the photograph presented by the Prosecution is self-evident, and the Defence does not dispute that it was made from Room 22. We can see only a small, tiny part of the upper arch of the bridge, and the witness is showing a house, and this is not explained very precisely in the transcript, which is on the slope on the opposite bank. And he said he could see this tiny bit of the arch of the bridge, and this is quite sufficient for the Defence and we don't see any need to show him our photographs. Since the Defence has already made them, we can show him a photograph made from the annex. We have, for instance, a photograph from Room 23, which, as you remember, was contested, that is, the left wing, marked with number 3; and we have a photograph from Room 22, the annex. That's what we can show him, although he claims that he had not been in the annex but in the part which he has just shown us on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've made it very clear. Thank you very much, indeed. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, the soldiers from Serbia, how long did they stay in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Almost two weeks. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After these two weeks, before the soldiers from Serbia left, did anyone tell you what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. I went out to work for people from Serbia proper, and one of those Serbs told me, "We are leaving tomorrow, and your fate will depend on the Serbs who are going to come now. To me, you are all Turks and you are all the same to me."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he indicate what may happen to you and the other detainees? Did he indicate anything?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, yes, he did. I was working then with the Witness 54. He said something like, "They will try you. They will know which ones among you are good, which are bad. Simply, they will define where we belong, to which category."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he mention any category?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He didn't say three groups, but he did say we will be categorised, and that was down to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you were working at that time with Witness 54. What were you doing? What were you asked to do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I know that there had been snow. As they were entering the building, there was an office with a furnace where correction officers were before the war, and then I was supposed to chop firewood and prepare it for the furnace.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the soldiers from Serbia left, on that day, who took over from them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The Serbs from Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened -- whom did you see come to the KP Dom after the Serbs left, the Serbs from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: In the evening we got some kind of small sandwiches, and in the morning when I got up, I don't know whether it was 9.00, 10.00, I saw in the compound quite a few people I knew in uniform, in the former KP Dom guard uniforms. And also there were some in military uniforms and they started shuffling about. So this was between the prison building and the kitchen, actually, that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Whom did you recognise walking there in this space?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Am I supposed to mention names?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I recognised people I knew from before, Milenko Cancar, inter alia, then Milivoj Maric, then Rasevic. Then I saw that Mila Krnojelac. That's what they called him, Mila, Milorad. That's the first time I found out what his name was. I can't remember right now. Oh, yes, Slavko Koroman. Give me some more time and I'll remember more people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let us first speak about the people that you just mentioned. Mr. Cancar, Milenko Cancar, you said. Was he a guard in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: All these people I saw, 90 per cent of them were guards. I knew them from before. Milenko was a guard before the war. Milenko is his name for sure. I'm not sure whether it's his surname, though, Cancar, but I think it is. He was sort of a biggish man. Then also there was Slavko Koroman.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Milenko Cancar is number 26 on P -- on this list of employees, P-3, Slavko Koroman is number 32, and a Maric, Milivoj, is under -- listed under --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Mara?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, Maric, Mara, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's number 102.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mara, is this a nickname? It doesn't sound like a proper name.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, Mara is a nickname. That's what I called him, Mara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you then asserting that it was the one that you referred to, the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because there's no other possibility, at least not according to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Rasevic. What was he wearing, and did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him from before. It's not that I talked to him very much, but I knew him. He also had a KP Dom uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Todovic, Savo Todovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but right at that moment I didn't know it was Savo Todovic. But I saw him. I knew him by sight, but I didn't know that Savo Todovic was his name. That I found out later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what was he wearing? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It seems to be coming back to my mind that he was a civilian, but I really don't know, actually. I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you saw Mr. Krnojelac, and you said that you didn't know his first name at that time, Milorad Krnojelac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, right. I knew that man, because I worked with his son for a long time. I knew him and I came to that cafe restaurant when it was being built, so I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that you knew his sons. How many sons does he have and which of the sons do you know from before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, maybe I'll make a mistake. He had either three or four sons. He had to have had three sons, but he might have had four too. I knew one called Dubravko, Dubravko or Jadranko. That's the one who worked with me, and I think that was his oldest son. He worked with me in Ozren for at least ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said you came to that cafe restaurant. What cafe restaurant do you mean? To which restaurant or cafe did you go related to the Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: That's in the house. His brother or both of them together. I don't know. When they were building that cafe, they needed my services, because I'm a welder, for their boiler or something like that. He asked me to fix some of their pipes, and I went over there to see how I could have those pipes made.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who ran this cafe in the Krnojelac house? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: One of the sons. One of the sons was an owner, probably. I mean, I never really asked. I just went there to help, to help Jadranko or, rather, Dubravko.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, was he involved in politics? Do you know? Before the war, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I have no idea whatsoever about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Krnojelac had a function in the reserve army?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think he had to be somewhere, either in the civil defence or in the reserve force, like I was, but I don't know about this related to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw him on that first day in the KP Dom, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, when I saw him, he had his back turned to me, so I didn't know it was him. But then he turned around, and then I realised that I recognised him, and I thought I knew this man. This was Dubravko's father. He was wearing military uniform, winter uniform. We who did our military service knew what winter uniforms were and what summer uniforms were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What does a winter uniform look like? What colour does it have and what distinguishes it from the summer uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, it's like looking at a civilian winter coat and a summer coat. I don't know how to explain this. I don't know how to explain it, but when I see it, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of colour does the uniform have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Olive-green/grey.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is it the old SMB uniform that the JNA had?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Now you've really got me confused. What do you mean, "old"? It is a military uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you see any insignia on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: As far as I could see then, I saw that he had some kind of a belt with shoulder straps. We, as soldiers, knew that this would be an officer Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or an NCO wearing that. I also saw that he had a pistol on his belt, just like other soldiers did. It was closed in something. How should I put this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This kind of belt with shoulder straps, what colour does it have and what does it look like? Can you explain it a little bit more detailed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I could a bit. It's a belt. It's made nicely, and the colour could be, well, mauve. Well, there's nothing else I can really say. Take the picture of any officer, take a look at it; that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How is this belt worn? Is it on the waist or is it over the ... How do you wear this? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Soldiers wore it with two straps, while the officers wore a big strap that goes from left to right or from right to left. I don't know. It goes from the shoulder to the opposite hip, so it either goes from the right shoulder to the left hip or from the left shoulder to the right hip.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did Mr. Krnojelac have this officer-style belt that you just explained, going from the shoulder to the hip?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that he had a pistol. Did he have anything else on his body, on the belt?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think that there was a bag on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of bag? Is that something very typical?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Leather. Leather bag. An ordinary leather bag, I think, military bag, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is it a bag that all soldiers wear or is that related to officers only?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, both could wear it in our situation; however, it is usually squad leaders who wore it, corporals.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know at that time when you saw him for the first time what position he had in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Nobody knew that. They walked about there. The Serbs from Serbia said that our people would be coming in, and then we looked through the window to see who would recognise who, but I didn't really know anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Krnojelac and the other people, when you saw them in the yard, where were you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Room 11, the one that faces the corridor and the kitchen. If you have a picture, I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the photo 7479.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It's this part here where they were moving about, this part, approximately. This is mainly the area where they were, over here. And now here is Room 11. You could see from there. So this is the view from Room 11, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I didn't see what he was pointing to. It may have been on the other photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. The witness was pointing at the yard, the main yard in front of the staircase on the photo, right in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He was actually pointing to something that is not on the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is, where you were. That is actually the view. What you see here, is that the view that you had from your Room 11?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. Yes. But I showed Room 11 to be here, behind this, and from that room I could see this, precisely this. This is what I could see from Room 11. This is what I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness was actually pointing at Room 11, which is not on the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did any of these people that you saw in the yard come to the room on that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, they did, after I don't know how much time. I think one of the guards came to the room, Savo Todovic came, Rasevic, and Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they all come together?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, they did; at least, that's the way I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did they talk to the detainees, that is, to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Not to me personally, but to other inmates. I think, as far as I can remember, that Krnojelac did not make a speech. Rasevic made a speech. He told us that we were citizens, isolated citizens, without any rights, something to that effect. That was the definition, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you or any of the other detainees, did you respond to this, that you were there without rights? Did anybody say something?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. There was a polemic, a bit of a quarrel. It was said that we were civilians, that we weren't to be blamed for everything. I remember well, but I don't remember who said it, whether it was Savo Todovic, Rasevic, or Krnojelac who said this, that those were orders issued by some kind of command, that these were orders and that they could not make any further comments with regard to that, that we were isolated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When this discussion took place, did anybody mention what kind of command it was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: We all knew, all of us inmates. When the command was mentioned, what the command was. If they were leading Serb personalities, then that was the command. Nobody asked who the commander was, because we all knew who the commander was, the group of people commanding a state.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you know that? You said that everybody knew. How did you learn that there was a command?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, okay. I find this question to be a bit strange, but ... Everybody did their military service in the Yugoslav People's Army, in the JNA, and the command is a group of people that commands the people. We know that. Before the war, we knew about the SDA and the SDS and we knew that the people of the SDS were leaders who were commanding the Serbs and then on the other side there were these other commanders. And we knew the names. I knew Velibor Ostojic, Vojo Maksimovic. Before the war they were the leading personalities there and they were the ones who were commanding then. We knew. We all knew that. I mean, how should I put that to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the KP Dom staff took over, how many detainees were you in Room 11 and all together? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: According to information which is only approximate, perhaps it's not accurate, in my Room 11 there was between 100 and 110 persons, and then also, according to the information we had, which was a bit scarce, it was about 300, 350 people all together, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the time passed, the following weeks, did the number of detainees increase? Were more detainees coming in?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it increased.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is your estimate of the highest numbers of detainees at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, according to our Sunday counts from the window, when people were going out for breakfast or lunch, the count seems to range between 600 and 615.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those detainees in your room, what ethnicity did they have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Muslims. There was one Croat too, or rather a Catholic. I don't know whether he's a Croat too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were there Serb prisoners in the KP Dom as well?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were Serbs detained in the KP Dom as well at a later stage or at that time already?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: There were about four or five detainees who had remained from before the war. They were convicts, though. But I mean, I was not a detainee; I was an inmate. So you have to distinguish between the camp and the prison. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were there Serbs? You said there were a few convicts in the prison. Where were they kept? Were they in the same room as the Muslims or separate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: They were separate. Muslims were not allowed access to them, nor were they allowed access to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where were they kept? Where in the prison compound?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: There were four of them left, I think. They worked in the kitchen then. They had been convicted. When you enter the KP Dom, they were on the right-hand side, the building we mentioned, precisely in that area, 22, 23. And then they were either up in 22 or a bit lower, but they were there. And I think that they were on the first floor of this building on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did at a later point in time during your detention, did more Serbs -- did Serb prisoners arrive?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Some kind of politicians arrived and they told us that they were from Banja Luka and Trebinje, and there were Serbs from Foca. Yes, they were coming in. Some were leaving after a while, others were staying longer. Yes, they were coming in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Serb prisoners, were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think -- I mean, I saw quite a few of them in civilian -- in military uniforms, but also in civilian uniforms. But then what they were, I didn't really ask them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall that reporters once entered the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did they come?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think it was June, July. I do not remember dates. I didn't really want to know them either, so you have to appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What year was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you talk with these journalists?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, with a journalist. I think he was from Serbia, from Belgrade, I think, judging by his accent. I also talked to some Frenchman.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You want the shorter version of that as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: They asked me why I was here in prison, or rather, here in camp. Then I said that I didn't know, just because I was a Muslim. And that's what the Frenchman asked me. I told them all of that in the French language because Slavko Koroman allowed me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they ask you if -- did any of them ask you if you were caught -- captured during battle?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. The gentleman asked me where I had been captured, and I told him that I had not been captured at all and that he cannot put it that way. That's a mistake. I was brought in. It's not that I was running away or something like that. And I distinguish between the two, to be captured and to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that Slavko Koroman was present. Was anyone else present from the prison staff when you had this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't know exactly. However, these French journalists were there and those journalists from Serbia too. I think they introduced themselves as being from the Borba newspaper, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I asked you -- actually, I asked you about the prison staff members present. Was someone there besides Mr. Koroman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Slavko Koroman is this guard, officer, whatever you call him, and then there were the journalists and then probably over there there must have been somebody else, but I was in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Those Exhibits P448 and 448/A will be under seal. They do reveal the man's address. Right. We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned already that in this short period when the Serbian soldiers were in the camp that you worked for them. Did you work when the regular prison staff ran the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I arrived on the 18th of April. I think I started working in end April or early May, I believe. I cannot tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did this come about that you started to work? Who told you that you should work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't know who told me, but I was called by a guard to come downstairs, so I did, and I met directly with Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you meet Mr. Rasevic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Right in the hallway. When you are about to leave the KP Dom, through that iron door, there is the reception area nearby and the door. It's a small hallway. You could go to the left or to the right from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I would like to show the witness Exhibit 6/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, can you orient yourself with this floor plan and point out where you were taken to Mr. Rasevic, where you met him.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: This area here, where I'm pointing right now. At least, that's what I think, according to this picture. If this is the gate, the entrance door from the outside, and this is the iron door, then this is the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing at this passageway after the entrance to the KP Dom from the street side, the reception. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did Mr. Rasevic tell you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He told me that I should work for him, that I should start working there. I don't know whether I had mentioned it in my statement earlier, but he asked whether I had any quarrel with a certain Serb, and with regard to any of the Serbs I knew, I had no quarrel whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he explain why he wanted to know if you had quarrels with Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He didn't explain really, but I could understand in a way. I could deduce why he told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Because I was supposed to work outside the KP Dom, and it was out of concern for my protection, safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you had this conversation with Mr. Rasevic, did anyone else join you or was anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac came up in the meantime. He came along in this hallway. There were more senior officers in the hallway. He said I would be working for the KP Dom, that is, Rasevic said that to Krnojelac. Krnojelac, I believe, nodded his head and he didn't say anything. He made no comments. I don't think I heard him say anything. But he did stop there for a while, as if he were thinking whether that would be all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On this occasion, did you already know that Mr. Krnojelac -- what position Mr. Krnojelac had in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't even know what he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did Mr. Rasevic address Mr. Krnojelac? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think he called him Krnojelac. That's at least what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you learn about the position of Mr. Krnojelac, if ever?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, about Krnojelac's position, there are several versions. I'll tell you about one of them. After a brief period spent in the KP Dom, I asked Savo Todovic whether I could write an application, a sort of request, something to the effect why I was here and could I get out. And he said yes. And since I could only write in Latinic script, I didn't know the Cyrillic, he allowed me to do so and I said I'd bring my request the next day. A certain man, I believe his name was Jasarevic wrote out this request for me in Cyrillic and I handed it to Savo and Savo said, "I'll hand it over to the warden to take it to the command for review, and then we'll see what will happen." Then he mentioned the warden, but he didn't say the Warden Krnojelac or anything; he just said "the warden." So I knew there was a warden at the KP Dom. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why would you have to write it in Cyrillic? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: That's a funny question. Nobody told me that. It's just that when I arrived at the KP Dom, and even before the war started, the Serbs used the Cyrillic. It's their script. And since they started calling it the Serbian Republic, it was something that I decided for myself that I wanted to write it in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you write, or rather this other person who helped you? What did you write? What kind of a request?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I cannot explain it verbatim, but I can tell you what the essence was. "I kindly request the command," and then in brackets, "the competent authorities," or something, "to release me, because I do not feel guilty and I believe I am locked up here, although innocent, and I am requesting to be released from the camp."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Todovic told you that you could write something to this effect. Why did you address it to the command and not to the warden?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Because, as I have said once already, when they first came to our room, they told us that we were isolated citizens there who have no rights whatsoever and that they were executing orders given them by the command. That's why I understood that we were in the hands of some command, and that's the picture that we had. Even before, when I was talking to Savo, Savo told me that all they were doing -- it's actually the people from outside who were doing it, and they were mentioning this command all the time, the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Todovic tell you what he would do with this letter, with this written request?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I've just said it. He said he would hand it over to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever get a reaction, an answer to your request?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In what format was it? Was it a written answer or how was it answered?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: On one occasion when I was working at the metalwork shop, Savo Todovic came along with an ugly grin, and he motioned me to approach him, and he said, "Your request was thrown into the waste bin." And he mentioned some man Damjanovic, who had run away from Foca to Pljevlje. In any case, he told me my request was basketed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you write this request, and when did Mr. Todovic inform you that it was in the wastepaper bin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think I wrote my request at the beginning, when I started working, so it could have been May. And it was denied sometime in end June or early July. I couldn't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did other detainees start to work with you in end of April/beginning May?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there actually a working group of people that continuously worked?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think right at the beginning this metal workers' group was formed, and it always numbered between 7 and 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were there other groups of workers who did something different from you, you 15?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: There were not perhaps groups exactly, but they took out people occasionally to sweep the yard, to work at the kitchen and do odd jobs around Foca, like transporting flour. They would go occasionally, right at the outset, and later a separate group was formed to work at the farm, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many detainees worked all together, if you would put a number to the people who would work? Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: From day to day, that would change. Groups would increase or be reduced. But the maximum number of people who were working at the camp was between 50 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was work voluntary?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could call it voluntary in a sense, but I would like to define that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I'll give you an example.
