If you're locked up in an area out of which you cannot get at all, and if somebody offers you work, then it's always better for you to get outside and work, because you can expect to get some things like food, cigarettes, even contacts with Serbs and find out something. It's better than staying in the room. So in a way you can call it voluntary, although in another sense it is quite ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you paid for your work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Sometimes in cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What does it mean, sometimes in cigarettes? How many cigarettes did you get for your work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Depending on the day, depending on the month, and depending on the goodwill of those who gave us cigarettes, we would get five or ten. The factory which produced them had some sort of refuse cigarettes which were substandard or non-standard. They were not a standard length, for instance. And they were going to waste anyway, so they gave them to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who gave these cigarettes to you? The prison staff or people from outside?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I personally got them from my so-called superior, who was in charge there. That was Relja Golijanin. And sometimes the superior officers who guarded us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Golijanin is listed under number 40 in P-3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The work, did this have other advantages besides getting cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You mean me personally or the group which worked with me?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. All of you. Did you get additional food?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. We all got extra food. We called it snacks. That was between lunch and supper.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did it include?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It varied. I think it was a piece of bread with butter or margarine on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned already that it was favourable to get out of the room and to work. Did working help you survive the conditions in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It helped me personally very much because I could get more food and better food than what we officially got in our rations. I could get more cigarettes. It was good for me personally. I liked working, at least, better than staying inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that Mr. Rasevic personally talked to you about starting to work. How did the other detainees that later worked start to work? Do you know that? How did they get into the working group?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I have no proof, but I can assume. In fact, that's how it should be, because it can't be any other way, considering that before that, up until June, I believe, everyone had already gone through those interrogations by interrogators who came from outside, who didn't work at the KP Dom, but came from Foca. Based on those statements and on the statements of Serbs who knew these people personally, they decided who would work and who wouldn't. They decided whom they could believe and whom they couldn't. This is at least what I thought, and I believe it is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with a Mr. Slavko Ivanovic to this effect?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Now, who is Slavo Ivanovic? Oh, yes, yes. Yes, of course I know him. Yes. On one occasion I did talk to him, when I was going to the hotel. There was the Serbian national cuisine there and I was making a platform and awning for that kitchen. Slavko Ivanovic approached me. He was holding an automatic gun in his hands. He had a parting in his hair. He dismissed the guard, saying, "I know this man, and there's nothing wrong with him." He said that, "You got a positive assessment also from the company where you worked, and all of you who are working are protected." That's approximately what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you have this conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: That could have been June, maybe mid-June, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Slavko Ivanovic from before the war, and who was he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I could spend hours talking about him. I knew him and his entire family, all of them, but I don't think you want to hear that. I will just say that for a while he and his family were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This conversation that you had with him, how did it start, actually? What was the reason to talk about this? How did it start?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Slavko Ivanovic just happened to be going towards the hotel by chance, and he saw me there. That's probably how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And try to remember: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You mean in addition? Yes, I think I can remember. He said, "Listen, Lija, there will be no problems. I think when Gorazde falls, all of you will be released." That's what I remember him saying. There may be something else, but I cannot recall now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that he actually said that you who are working are protected. Did he say why you were protected and by whom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I gave you the brief version just now, but he said there was a meeting in Cohodar Mahala where the names of prisoners, or rather, inmates, were read out, those who were up there. I just said that I got a positive assessment from Ozren, and I meant that I got a reply to the effect that I'm a good, honest man. And I got the same kind of positive assessment or reply from Cohodar Mahala, which means that it was written somewhere that in view of the existing Serbian state, it could be considered that I was not against it, that state.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he tell you when this meeting in Cohodar Mahala had taken place and who took part in it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He said a few days ago there was this meeting. I don't remember him mentioning who had been present. I cannot recall now. Maybe it's in one of my statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that he mentioned that they discussed on this meeting the inmates or prisoners. Which prisoners? You mean those in the KP Dom in general? Did he say something?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I have just remembered. He said they had a meeting and that they discussed Muslims. They investigated who was who. I don't know how to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's discuss the proceedings involved with the work. What happened when you were taken out for work for the first time? If you can explain to us the steps that were taken.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I worked for three years, and I don't know what you want me to explain, about a particular day or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your first day, were you called out from your room to go to work or how did this start?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I had one pair of trousers and one military shirt, which I put on, and I left with a man called Jovo. I can't remember his last name now. He used to work as an electrician at the KP Dom before, with a man named Susnjevic. We were going to dismantle a door from a house and install it elsewhere in a house in Donje Polje. That was earlier in the day, in the morning, before lunch. Then I went to the metalwork shop, where I broke padlocks, because before that there had been workers in the workshop who had their own tools and they had locked them up, and there were no keys available. So I was supposed to take off the padlocks in order to enable them to take out the tools and sort them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Jovo actually call you out from Room 11, or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Nobody ever knew who had called them out, because there was one guard inside and one older guard outside. So the one inside would tell you to go to the iron door, and you would go there, ring a bell, and then another guard would take you over; and then a third man would take you wherever you were supposed to go. So it was like that when I was called out to go with Jovo and dismantle that door.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you reached -- when you passed the metal door that you just mentioned, did anyone put your particulars down and made a note that you were leaving, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I saw what had happened to me. Usually the one who was at the reception room, the one on duty, would record my name, because I know that this Jovo said, "Lija is coming with me." So he wrote it down and I went with him. So he did record my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did he write it down? What kind of paper was it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: This is a little window opening, and then through it he says he's coming with me. I did not go in through that little window opening to see what he was writing down, whatever. In fact, I was registered. Then this man at the reception office knew that I had gone there to work. Now, how? Well, you know, I was in a camp, so I can't really make comments to that effect. I mean, I didn't dare to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you returned, was another note taken? Was this registered as well when you returned after work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: When I came back -- I mean, usually Jovo would -- actually, at the reception gate, the guards would usually change, and then Jovo would say -- I mean, I'm just giving you an example. He would say, "I'm taking Lisica back. He's going to the compound." He would search me and then I would go into the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned Jovo, an electrician. Was he a staff member, was he a guard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You know what? At the KP Dom, when they established that KP Dom, actually, before he had worked as an electrician, and after that they were all actually guards; whereas, those who were electricians did both jobs, both one and the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean this Jovo was already working in the KP Dom as an electrician before the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know his last name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I can't really remember. Why don't you ask Krnojelac? Maybe he remembers. I can't remember exactly. Actually, if I thought about it more, maybe I could remember, but I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have too many Jovos on the list. We can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many days a week did you have to work? Did you have a five-days week, six-days week?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It was not always the same. Sometimes five, sometimes six, sometimes seven, sometimes three. Well, if we were to make an approximation, it could have been five days a week. There would be less and there would be more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you occasionally had to work on weekends as well?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have regular working hours?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The working hours for the metal shop were from 7.00 until 3.30, or until 3.00. However, since I worked all over Foca, sometimes in the hospital too, sometimes I'd stay until 5.00. It depended on the job that had to be done, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also have to work during night-time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Only once?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Once I went to work during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about the breaks? Did you have regular breaks during your work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: We had some regular breaks, and then it would really depend on the guards. If the guards were nasty, then we would have regular breaks; but if it was a good guard, then we would have more than the regular breaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What were the regular breaks? How many breaks did you have during Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a working day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Between 7.00 and 12.00 we had one break for the snack. It could have been around 10.00, about half an hour. That was half an hour. And then I think we had an hour for lunch. And since we went home, I mean, back to the camp, at 3.00, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This one-hour lunch break, when did you have this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, listen. First when I just started working, it wasn't an established working group of the metal shop. They would call people out from rooms and then people would go from the metal shop. We would be the first or sometimes the last to have our meals, so we would go at 12.00 to the compound and then we would go back and then we would go back home at 3.00. But then, after that, when we established -- when the working group was established, then after this break at 10.00 we would have yet another break just before the end of working hours. We would go and have a meal and that would mean that our work would be over.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you actually worked all through your time in the KP Dom. Were there times that you were not able to go out and work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You mean was I sick or something?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. That nobody went out. Were there times that nobody would go out for work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, there were such periods. I think there was one, two, or three, or perhaps even more than that. I can't remember. We would usually know when there was mobilisation, a state of alert, or something, probably when there was fighting around Gorazde, outside Foca. When there were bigger wars going on, then they would lock us up and wouldn't let us go out and work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know who made this decision that you couldn't go out for work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I have no written proof, but I have proof from the guards, when I asked the guards what's going on, and they said there's a big offensive against Gorazde and the command issued orders that nobody could go out and work. Guards told me about this. I was somehow on good terms with them and they made statements to that effect to me. Whether they were true or not, that I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During such an alert situation when nobody worked, did you work nevertheless, on one occasion? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. It so happened, I don't know exactly, but I saw those corpses. Probably the Muslims carried out to slaughter, massacre, somewhere in Ustikolina, and they brought them to hospital. And I had not finished some kind of water pipes for the heating between the two buildings. Then there was a state of alert and they called me to finish that, and when I came down to the hall, the same Rasevic said to me -- no. I think it was Relja Golijanin and not Rasevic. I'm sorry. That they should call the command to ask whether they should give me permission to go and finish that. I came back to the iron gate and I waited there, and after I don't know how much time, Golijanin came back and said that they got permission, and he went up to Mr. Krnojelac's to see. And I went to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that he went up to Mr. Krnojelac's to see. What do you mean? What did he say to you, Mr. Golijanin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He said to me? He said to me, as far as I can remember, "I'm going to the warden to see because the command has forbidden people to go out and work. I'm going to see with him whether you can go and finish this part of the hospital," the one I was supposed to do, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When he returned, did Mr. Golijanin -- when he returned, did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, he did. He called me and, and some Davidovic came from the hospital, one who would drive me to the hospital. He said that he had received permission from the command that I could go out and work, that he got permission, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Relja Golijanin, you mentioned that he was your supervisor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Golijanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Golijanin. Sorry. You mentioned that he was your supervisor. Did you get all your tasks from him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Throughout my stay he was my supervisor, and I got it from him. From time to time he would tell me -- well, I had a special job. I mean, I was a welder and I had these oxygen bottles and they were very scarce, so they had to be taken care of. And sometimes these wardens --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: -- guards would come and they would ask for me to do something for them using these oxygen bottles. Then he said to me, "I cannot turn anyone down, you know." When he would be away for two or three days, he would say, "You are not allowed to weld anything without me. Only the warden and I can give you orders, nobody else."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the warden give you orders in relation to welding?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I remember once that I was supposed to do something, I don't know what, and I said that to the guard. I said that I wouldn't do that. I mean, it's not that I would not do it, but I don't dare do it, because I would suffer consequences, that that is what Golijanin told me. And he went to the warden's. That's what I called him. And then the warden once came to the metalwork shop. He said, "Lija, you can do that."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did this happen that the warden came to you and said, "Lija, you can do that"? Can you place it in a time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, it could be 1993 or perhaps the end of 1992. Sometime during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the warden?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I knew that the warden was Krnojelac, but I did not read that anywhere, nor did I see it written anywhere. I personally addressed him that way sometimes, because I would see him and I would usually say, "Warden, what do I do about this? What do I do about that?" And he would say to me, "Ask Relja," or I don't know, "Do what you want," or he would tell me do this or do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did anyone from the prison staff ever tell you that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, the guards, when there was something -- well, they'd say warden, but they wouldn't say warden Krnojelac. They would say, "We're going to see the warden," or if they were to have meetings, they would say, "We're going to the warden's." And this same Relja said to me, the warden this, the warden that. As for Mr. Krnojelac, I saw him there often and I was in contact with him. I was certain that he was the warden.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that you actually worked in various places about the town, and you already mentioned that you worked in the Hotel Zelengora.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you worked in the Hotel Zelengora, did you ever see Mr. Krnojelac there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he doing there? Could you see?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: What was he doing? I don't know. But I do know, when I was working on this cauldron that was to be used for cooking, that he came by once. He did not talk much, it seemed, but he nodded and then went to the building, the hotel. But what he was doing there, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you worked at the Hotel Zelengora or at other places all over the town, were you guarded?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: 99 per cent. Yes, 99 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who guarded you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Usually I was guarded by guards from the KP Dom. Sometimes -- I mean, once I worked for the military police, and then the military police came. Rasevic was there then, and he asked me whether I knew the policeman and I said I did and then I went to work with this policeman and then the same policeman drove me there and drove me back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that you worked for the military police. Where did you work for the military police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, maybe I didn't express myself right when I said for the military police. In the hotel there was this police. I call them the military police because they were the police. I went there to stack up some sacks for them. I went together with Mr. Ekrem Zekovic. We went there to unload some things. I think it had something to do with food and hygiene. We were unloading this from a truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean the military police or police was in the Hotel Zelengora, stationed there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee, but while I was there there were several of them who told me where I should leave these things, where I should unload them. Now, whether they were stationed there or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you ever taken to the Velecevo women's prison for work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I went there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of work did you have to do there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Frames for a kiosk, something that had to do with a kiosk.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Velecevo women's prison, for what was it used during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't know what its function was, but I saw quite a few soldiers when I was there. I think it was -- I mean, this is my opinion. This was some kind of a technical platoon or something. I think the military was there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have to repair military vehicles when you went to Velecevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, once. I had to fix some kind of screws on a military vehicle. Spica was there, that was his nickname, Radovic. We went to school together. And yes, I think I cut off two or three screws.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was that the only military vehicle that you worked on, or did you work on several?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. I worked on another occasion, but that was at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you worked at Velecevo, did you ever see high-ranking military leaders there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think so. I think that's the way it was. While I was up there at the kiosk -- I mean, I knew this Velibor Ostojic, so I think I saw him and Vojo Maksimovic, and Miro Stanic, because I knew this Miro Stanic through the hosiery factory, through the man who was his driver. Actually, he wasn't his driver. He drove a Deutz. I think I saw them together. I mean that's as far as I could know him. I knew Velibor Ostojic. He was a plumpish man. I think I saw him and I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I had actually asked you if you saw high-ranking military leaders, and you gave their names. Were they military leaders at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, that's a good question, you know, but I was not in the Serb command. But I saw them because I knew them. I knew who these people were. I don't know them. I mean, I was not a commander, a Serb commander. I was not a member of this military command, but we all knew that Velibor Ostojic, Miro Stanic, that they were the top people. Whether they were the real people, that I don't know, but you know, I was in a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Boro Ivanovic at Velecevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what position he had in the military, and did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I knew him from before just like that, just by sight, and sometimes we had contacts perhaps in relation to Godijevno where he was from. I heard, though, and I don't know whether my information was correct, that he had something to do with our exchange. I don't know what his function was, whether he was some kind of a commander or something. I don't know. But I would often see him coming to the KP Dom. Why he came, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he a teacher?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think he was. He had something to do with the school. He did teach at the school, but what kind of teacher he was exactly, primary school, secondary school, or something, whether he was a professor, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw him at Velecevo or in the KP Dom, what was he wearing? Was he in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He had a camouflage uniform. It was a bit sloppy. It wasn't very tidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where else in the town did you work? You have already mentioned now a few locations. Where else did you work? Did you ever work in a grocery store?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: In a shop. Yes, I worked in two shops.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What two shops were they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I worked in a shop where the glass had been broken. This shop was supposed to be opened. I don't think it had been opened before that, and it was supposed to sell food.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it a shop related to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, yes. Before the war this shop was the KP Dom's in part, or I don't know exactly. But before the war the KP Dom farm sold milk, cheese, and then they distributed that. The KP Dom continued delivering milk and such products in shops in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see these shops actually start functioning as a shop later on?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: I would go to Velecevo for five or six days and I would take the little TAM truck and then we would get milk or rather empty milk bottles from these shops. Since we collected these empty bottles every morning, they probably worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned another shop that you worked in. What kind of shop was this? Who was the owner?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You mean who was the owner during the war or before the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Both, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, before the war I think it was Perucica, and after the war I guess the Serb Republic, or perhaps the KP Dom also rented it out. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why do you think the KP Dom rented it out? Was there any connection with the KP Dom that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, because the KP Dom was involved in agriculture up there at the farm they made their own produce, dairy products, pig and chicken products. We tried to make some kind of shelves and things there so that people could sell this produce and they could make money. How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you work in the two shops that you mentioned? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, that was also June, July.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. I think that Aladza was in 1993 and the other one was 1992. Quite a bit of time went by between the two shops in terms of when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that you worked in the Foca hospital. In which time periods did you work in the Foca hospital? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I remember, yes, from 1992 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean throughout you went there quite often, then, or what?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Quite frequently. Maybe if I look at the time I spent there, then it was perhaps four months running, but it was in the period between 1992 and 1994, with intervals. It was rather frequent.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I mentioned that I was a welder by occupation, so I welded and did all the jobs related to metalwork, everything that had to do with metal jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you went to the hospital for work, did you sometimes take medications from the hospital back to the KP Dom for detainees?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I had quite a few offers from our inmates, because I used to go down there and they would ask me, "Please bring this or that medicine." And I even carried letters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you ever caught while doing that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Once, I don't know why. Maybe I was stupid or I was under great tension - I didn't want to work any more. I just stopped and said, "I'm not going to work any more, and kill me if you want." And then Relja Golijanin told me to return all the tools or whatever I was issued with, and I said, "I have nothing." And they searched me and they found a letter I was supposed to take to some doctor, a relative of one of the Muslims, [redacted], and the doctor's name was Cele.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you punished for carrying this letter on you or for refusing to work in any way?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: At the moment when I accepted, I regretted it, that very moment, but it was all done already and I had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I do not really understand your answer. My question was: Were you punished for carrying this letter or for refusing to work in any way, and it says in the English transcript: "At the moment when I accepted it, I regretted it." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Had I refused that order, I knew straight away that I was in trouble, and I regretted it because I knew there would be very hard consequences. And this letter Cancar found on me, he took it to Mitar Rasevic or someone else, and I was taken to solitary confinement. And after a while I got out from this solitary confinement, and in this hallway Savo Todovic met me and he said he was aware of what I had said and what I had done.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you punished afterwards, and if so, through what means? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: From that moment on, I was trying to apologise, and he said, "Lija, do you know that Muslims are foes? Do you know what you're doing?" And he showed that letter to me. Behind me there was [redacted] [redacted] standing - I don't know which one of them - and he asked the question, the same question of this man, and he asked me, did I know what was written in that letter. Then he punished me. He said, "I think 20 days of solitary confinement." But I was going to work anyway. I think I actually spent three or four days in solitary confinement and then they released me back to my room and I started working again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever work on the house of Mr. Krnojelac during your confinement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, do you mean the date while I was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Approximately. I thought you were thinking about it. How often were you --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You want me to think about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. I thought you were thinking. How often did you work on the house? Do you know how many days all together?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think, if I could add it up, it was perhaps 15 to 20 working days, roughly, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know which year it was? Was it in 1992 or later, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I worked in 1992, but I also remember that I did some work in 1993 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In 1992 when you worked there, was it in the summer, autumn, or was it even winter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It was in autumn, the end of autumn/the beginning of winter. It was not the fiercest frost, but it wasn't warm either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you worked on the house, who took you there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you the only one working on the house or were other detainees working there together with you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I did only metal jobs, which means I made the staircase and the metal railing, the metal jobs involved there. But I saw other people working there as well, doing construction work. However, I worked mostly indoors, because I was making the staircase going from the ground floor upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you recall which other detainees worked there? And please use the list in front of you for those who are protected witnesses. Do you recall -- can you tell us the names or the numbers of other detainees who worked there on the same house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Together with me, 144 worked with me, and he was tied to me, 163 [as interpreted], Telo Mustafa, Telo Aziz, some other people as well. One [redacted] Those were the people who worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me just clarify something. In the transcript it says that 163 worked with you. There is no 163 on the list. Is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: There is 162. I cannot see 163 written anywhere. I don't know

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. It's not. Is it is a mistake in the transcript? Did you say, or did you want to say 162?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He didn't work with me. Only 144 and 73 worked with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No other people from this list. Maybe he did work, but I didn't see him. I have to explain it a little about this house. I worked indoors. I worked on the interior. On the outside there were other people whom I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Did Mr. Zekovic work with you on the house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I had forgotten about him. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who told you what you have to do in the house? Who gave you your jobs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: When I was supposed to do a job, or this guy under the code-name, who was a locksmith - he had more work to do, because I was a welder - this man under number 144. I would approach Relja Golijanin or Krnojelac's son. And on several occasions I stood there with Krnojelac and discussed with him directly things that were supposed to be done, what should be done and how, because he didn't know much about construction and the frames. But that was usually Relja's job.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you started to work there for the first time, did you have a discussion about what would have to be done, before you even went there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before you started to actually work in the house, did you discuss your job or the job of the other detainees? Was there a kind of a discussion, a broader discussion with the people involved in this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you went to the house for the first time, did you already know what you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Because before I would go to Krnojelac's house, I had to prepare my material, and the gentleman under number 144 went, because we worked with iron and pipes. We had to prepare this material, load it onto a car, and take it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that you got your tasks from Mr. Relja, and you also mentioned that you approached also Mr. Krnojelac's son. When did you approach them, and for what?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: That happened during that time I was working. When you are making a railing or a fence for somebody, it can happen easily that you do the job differently than the client wanted it, and then they say you have to change it. If you see that Krnojelac is around, you can say, "I have to change this. May I do it this way?" Or if Relja was there, I would talk to him. So in any case, you have to talk to an authorised person. If I was working on Krnojelac's house, then I thought his son was a person I could speak to, authorised, because there might be obstacles later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How often was Mr. Krnojelac's son at the work site?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: During my stay, I know about this Dubravko or Jadranko. I keep confusing this. I talked to this man often, because we were friends, and I was glad to see him. He was often there. He was a policeman. He would take a walk around and then come by.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was there another son as well on the work site that you could approach?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. I saw another one. I don't know whether he was the second or third son. I hadn't known him before, but he was pointed out to me and I was told that this was one of the warden's sons. Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you also approach him when something had to be clarified?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: [redacted]approached him instead, but I was present and I had a discussion with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How often did Mr. Krnojelac come to the work site?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He would come by together with Rasevic during the day. He and Rasevic would take off somewhere and then they would pass by the house, take a tour. Several days would pass without my seeing him and then he would come several times during one day. There was no rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you approach him also and talk with him about how to do the work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think I've just said that we had talked before we started. We discussed this work and we were giving him some suggestion, because Mr. Krnojelac had no clue about this metal staircase and about the construction, and he was asking us why things should be done in the way we were suggesting, et cetera, and then he would often come by to see how we were doing. And there was his wife as well. She would come by too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you worked on the house of Mr. Krnojelac, did you go back to the KP Dom for the meals, especially this snack?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We would take our breakfast usually in the morning and we received our food directly from the cook [as interpreted]. I once asked whether he had cooked it or whether it had been brought from somewhere. In any case, I know it was not KP Dom food.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you received -- "We received our food directly from the cook." What cook? What cook do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: What do you mean, "cook"?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I can only read what is in the English -- what I heard. It says in the transcript: "We would take our breakfast usually in the morning and we received our food directly from the cook."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake. It seems to be a hot meal. I misheard.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It must be a mistake of some sort. We received food, meals, from his sons. They brought us food directly to this house, and it was not food from the KP Dom. Other people, not me, would sometimes even have a brandy with them. I don't want to defend anyone, but at that moment food was much, much better than at the KP Dom. I don't know why was that, but in any case, we were pleased, and we preferred eating there at that house than at the KP Dom, because the food at the KP Dom was bland, completely. Maybe somebody misheard me. Maybe I meant the cook who had prepared the meal or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That clarifies the matter. Thank you. Did you have to work for Mr. Krnojelac or his son in any other place than the house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. I was making some sort of shelves in the metalwork shop for this son who had an accident. He was supposed to open a shop where the Planika shop used to be, and I was making these shelves so that this man, this other man, would take them there to install them. I was doing my job down at the metalwork shop and I was told that it was for his son. I don't know whether that's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you work on another work site related to the son who had the accident?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I didn't work, but once I went there to collect some paint, I think it was. It was Fehim Dedovic who did the paint job, and he personally told me that this work was being done for his son, who was disabled, that this apartment had been allocated to his son. And it had belonged to some Fadila, I believe he was a gynaecologist who had worked at the hospital. Sorry. It's not Fadila. It's Tafro.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The former owner of the apartment, was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually see the handicapped son in this apartment when you went there to pick up paint?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him up there, but when you ask me those things, you should understand: It's not that I really saw him. It was just a quick glance in passing. I was not interested. I was going about my business. But I did see him very quickly. I entered a corridor. There was a door open there. I saw him and I continued on my way. If somebody told me now that I was supposed to confirm an oath that it was him, I could hardly do it. It was just a passing glance. I can hardly claim with 100 per cent certainty that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of handicap did he have?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I heard on one occasion, I believe it was Krnojelac himself who told me, that he had lost both his legs when he stepped on a mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Krnojelac told you this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, Krnojelac must remember. He was supposed to make some sort of device for his child, for this son to exercise his arms, and he was at the metalwork shop. That's probably where we met. I was doing some job. And there was another man, Muhamed, who was speaking to him, and I was just present there. That was some kind of device for exercise. I think it was in 1993. You know, it's very hard when you're asking me about dates. I got things sorted out between 1992 and 1993, and I can distinguish between the years which were hardest for me and those which were less hard. Otherwise I cannot be much more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Krnojelac made this remark probably in the metalwork shop when this exercise machine was made. Did he come often to the -- no? Did he come often to the metalwork shop? Did you see Mr. Krnojelac often in the workshop?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you: I saw him almost every day. Perhaps not every day, but at least two or three times a week because there were cars about. In any case, I saw him often.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw him either in the metal shop or on the work sites where you met him, how did he behave towards you? How did he treat you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, as regards some guards, they could get a passing grade. As for others, he was decent towards me, but I didn't notice how he treated others. But for instance, when he was walking about, his face was not very -- was not very kind, so to speak. He didn't exactly invite people to address him. And people -- he came across as angry, sort of. People tried to avoid him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that you had several talks with Mr. Krnojelac and you addressed him as warden when you did so. Did you ever speak with him about the beatings and the disappearances in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion I asked him why I wasn't being exchanged, and I was telling him that the people who were locked up there were innocent. I said something like, "None of the people who are locked up here had been on the front line or in combat." He said, "I don't decide about such things." He said, tongue in cheek, "Lija, it's not me who locked you up." He said, "There were other people who decided such things," or he would say on a different occasion, "It's the command who is deciding." He said on one occasion, "Lija, I didn't lock you up," and something like, "I'm not the one to blame for this." I think he said, "There are other people," or maybe he said, "There is the command."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's difficult, but how often did you have such a conversation with him, and where and when? Was it only once?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: There was another occasion, and that ties in with my previous story. Krnojelac came by with Savo Todovic and I believe Rasevic was there as well, and they were going up there to the garage where Hamdo was working. And I approached them. I said I couldn't work any more. I was ravenous, I was going to faint. I told them how hard the work was on unloading. He turned away angrily and he brought me two slices of bread and he proffered them to me, saying, "I'm giving you this one and the commander is giving you the other one. That's all I can do to help you." I don't know what else happened, but that's approximately how it was that time. I don't think we made any further comments or that we discussed it any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the time has come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume at 2.30. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Lisica, before the break you described to us two conversations that you had with Mr. Krnojelac, and you mentioned the first conversation where you asked him if you could be exchanged, and where he mentioned that he was not the one to make this decision. Do you know when this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The end of 1992/beginning of 1993. Three, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did it take place? Where were you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think it could have been at the mechanic's shop, the metalwork shop, as it was called. Or it could have been at the farm. Wait a second. Wait a second. Let me think now. Wait. I think it was at the metalwork shop, after all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This other conversation where he gave you two slices of bread, you said that he was, he and Mr. Rasevic and Mr. Todovic were going up there to the garage where number 249 worked. Do you mean within this compound where the metal shop was? Do you mean this garage, or where?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. I mean if you have a drawing here, the metalwork shop was like right in front of the KP Dom, whereas the mechanic's garage was a bit further off. And all of that belongs to the same compound. Now, that could have been between the garage and the metalwork shop, but that is all one entity. I tried to be a bit more precise. That's why I'm putting it this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness Exhibit 6, the entire plan of the KP Dom compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Lisica, can you point out the metalwork shop where you usually worked and the garage that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I worked here. The heating room, the metalwork shop, and then all of this is sort of the metal complex. And the car mechanic's shop here belongs to that too. I'm pointing it out to you right now with this pointer. The story I told you might have taken place here where this little sign is. I don't know what this little sign means, but it could have been in this area. I don't know what this is. Is it something crossed out or something? It's probably a toilet. I think the toilet was there. The toilet was somewhere around here, so it could have happened here, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was indicating first showing his workplace and he was showing the boiler room, which is indicated as the boiler room in the plan, the metal shop in the middle and the metal shop next to the river. And he was referring to the garage he mentioned. He pointed to the auto mechanic's shop at the end of the compound, at the left end of the compound. For the place of the conversation, he pointed at this little square spot between the metalwork shop and the auto mechanic's shop. And I can't really read it on this small plan that I have if there is a toilet indicated in there, but it should be visible from the huge version. I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We can agree that it's the cross -- it's the square with the cross in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. It's enough with this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that you -- when you had this second conversation. When was it? Was it after the first one or earlier?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: This other conversation I had, I don't know whether I told you about it. There were several conversations. But then I had this one conversation by way of a joke, at the farm. And the other conversation was after this, when I talked about the exchange. When I talked about the exchange, that was -- I mean, we talked about this first thing and then this second one could have been a month, a month and a half later, 30 or 40 days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The first one, was it the discussion about the exchange or this incident where he gave you two pieces of bread? What was first?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The first conversation had to do with bread and hunger. The other conversation had to do with the exchange. And the third conversation, I don't know whether it was a conversation -- well, it wasn't that I joked with him. It was just like that. I was sort of relaxed. I really wonder why.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said this first conversation was about hunger, and you told us already in relation to this conversation that you told Mr. Krnojelac that were you going to faint. Did you actually speak about being hungry?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, okay. I wasn't fainting. I mean, I was just pretending because of him. But I was hungry. In all fairness, I was hungry. But it's not that I fainted or anything. I just pretended that I would faint so that I would get more food. I wasn't getting much food, no I was not. Nobody was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What exactly did you tell him? Did you complain about the small rations you got?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I said specifically Zeka was there and others, I think. I also think Mr. 144 was there too. I was cutting some boards for Maglic. And then I stopped him. I was doing this outdoors. I was doing it outdoors. And as I was working I saw them coming from up there, and then I turned off the tool and I said that I was hungry and that I wasn't getting enough food and that I couldn't do this and that also these gases were harmful and that welders would get milk and things like that, something in that sense. Do you want me to repeat everything I talked about?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Sorry. Yes, please. What else did you tell him? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I just said that. I asked for meals to be increased, that he should give me more to eat, and that was it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As a result -- as his answer, in addition to what you have already told us, do you recall anything else?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, wait a second. I don't know what he answered me. Maybe he remembers. I know that he turned around and that he brought two slices of bread. One was thicker and the other one was thinner. And it was also mentioned how many slices of bread were cut, that the command ordered 15 slices to be cut from one loaf of bread, and he was cutting 12 slices. And he was a bit upset. He was a bit angry. He said, "What more can I do?" And at that time when I would talk to him, I wouldn't dare say all the things I wanted to say. Because I tried to say everything but without any expense to me, so to speak. So that was the content of it, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that this has not been interpreted properly. The witness said, "I cannot help you with that." And in line 18 it says, "What can I do about it? What more can I do? What more can I do?" And the witness said, "I can't help you any."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I said something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you've got it recorded now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that you also had a third conversation with Mr. Krnojelac or a joke. You said on the Brioni farm. Did you have to work on the farm?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: We already said that once, whether I had to work. Of course I had to work, because I was in a camp. You asked me whether I volunteered. Yes, I had to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Wait. Wait. I wanted to know what kind of work did you have to do at the farm and how often did you work there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Excellent. Excellent. I went quite often. My task was to make these boxes for pigs, where pigs were kept. Pigs tend to break these up when they walk about. Then also chicken coops. When chicken coops would break, then I was supposed to weld them together. Everything that was made of metal at the farm, like fences, gates, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How often did you see Mr. Krnojelac at the farm when you worked there? Only one time or more often?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I saw him several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't know what he did. Sometimes he came with civilians. I did not know. He would walk around with them. Then sometimes he would come with Rasevic, sometimes he came with Savo, sometimes he came on his own. What he did, he walked around toward the place. I don't know. I didn't ask him what he did there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him with soldiers there or officers even?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, during my stay, while I was there, I actually did not see any big officers coming there anyway. They probably didn't come there at all. I don't know. I didn't see any. There were soldiers; that's true. But that there were some big and important people, no, I didn't see anybody like that. I don't know about these civilians, when they were walking around with him in civilian clothes. I didn't really pay that much attention. While I'm working, while I'm doing my job, I would look up and I would see him walking with someone. And it wasn't that you could dare stop all together and look and see what they were doing. You could just barely glance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said on one occasion you spoke with him at the farm. What was it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The farm is an area where the pig area was down, much lower. The Serbs at the time did not have enough food for pigs. They gave them apples. That means that it was autumn time. So they mixed these apples with bran and I was standing there. I don't know whether it was break time or whatever, so I was eating apples or rather looking at them because I wanted to get some of the better apples to take them with me. I said that, "There were pigs that weren't even touched by Muslims for a year and what do they do here? They feed apples to the pigs." I think he just laughed at that and that's the way it was

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you worked in the metalwork shop, did you have to service cars and vehicles of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. What do you mean, service.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is what I want to ask you. What did you do with the cars or with the vehicles? What were the tasks you had in relation to cars and other vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I worked as a welder before at the service shop, and I serviced trucks and vehicles in general. I was the one who helped mechanics and locksmiths. When a car would have a crash, an accident, when the exhaust pipe would break down, to cut screws, and then sometimes I would work a bit as a mechanic if I didn't have enough work as a welder. So even at that garage I worked a bit as a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the KP Dom have a small delivery truck, a Kedi?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. At first, as far as I know, because there was a warehouse underneath number 11, it was used for this food produce.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of a car was it? Can you tell us which brand it was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It was a Zastava 101. Instead of a back seat, it had sort of a big trunk.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did this car have a particular noisy exhaust pipe?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It didn't have anything special. It didn't have anything special, if you are referring to something special. However, it just had an exhaust pipe that wasn't good. It had a hole on it, so then the exhaust fumes were not regulated properly, so the sound was very loud.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever see bloodstains in this particular Kedi?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, once, in the back, Zeka and I were there. I saw stains on the bottom, on the floor, and on the sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was -- when did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You mean which month, year?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Which month, year, and what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It could have been approximately the month of July or August, mid-July/beginning of August. I'm not sure. And it was approximately in the morning, say around 9.00 or 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where was it parked when you saw it? Would you be able to point it out on the map that you just had in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, could the same plan be shown.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at a space in front of the metalwork shop, close to the Drina River, and he is pointing in the middle, approximately in the middle of this metalwork shop. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually have to clean this car on that same day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: When I finished the partitions that I was doing in the isolation cells, I had to take my tools there, so as I was taking the tools I had to see that. And then I came back. Zeka was taken back to the room and I returned to the metalwork shop by myself because I had to leave my tools because we had finished our work. Then somebody said to me there, I don't know who it was, a guard, and he said, "Lija, why don't you wash this, and then there's a toilet nearby, perhaps I can show it to you. I think it should be around here, right around here, the toilet." And then I took a hose and I washed this and then I went inside to the KP Dom, to the rooms there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I couldn't see where the witness was pointing at because I had to switch and I was too slow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you please point out where you got the water from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that you got a hose.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Here, where the toilet is. This is actually the metalwork shop, and behind it was a toilet, and there was water there too. I don't know whether this has been drawn precisely, but at any rate, it's in this area. It's in this area. I often used this water, and there was a hose there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the witness was pointing at the left end of the building that is marked as the metal shop close to the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you describe to us the sights of the bloodstains you saw and where they were within the car Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It was a stain roughly in the middle of this Kedi, of the trunk there, perhaps between 10 and 12 centimetres. That was the diameter. It wasn't round, actually. It wasn't -- it was sort of like this. And then it's on the left side or on the right side, if you look at it from the back, then on the right side. Yes, on the right side. The stain was there. It was like light red. I'm not saying anything. Well, that's the way it was. Well, like this big.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing in front of him in a circle, which was about 20 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you show it again?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Perhaps this big. This big. I mean, you know, [redacted] See, it's this big.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how much inches? I have difficulty to say how many inches?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Okay. Seven or 8 inches. Perhaps 7 or 8 inches. I don't know. You can measure it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Some of us are still impaired by imperial measurements, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it just this one bloodstain or was it -- did you see blood in other parts of this Kedi?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I told you, on the side, on the side, on the left and right side. But these are not such stains. They are smaller stains.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see anything else in the Kedi had you cleaned it? Was there something else besides the bloodstains?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Up in the corner there was a wire that had been on fire. And nothing else, I think. Oh, yes. There was a basket too, I think, and also this burned wire.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This burned wire, is it a particular sort of wire or was the wire burnt, burnt by fire? I'm just -- I don't really understand what you mean. Burnt wire, is that something particular, technical?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: In our language, burned wire means that it's a flexible wire, that you can't break it. It was used to tie things up in construction. It was good for that, for tying things up in construction, and we call it burned wire.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the guard who told you to wash the car, did he say anything about the bloodstains?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No, he didn't. How should I put this? When I took care of all this, he came up, he saw it, and he thought of telling me that, and I washed it and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you also have to service the warden's car?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Several times I cleaned his vehicle. I think it was a Yugo 45 or 55. It was red. Not exactly red, reddish. The colour is a bit strange. Yes, it was there often, and sometimes I'd bring it to the metalwork shop and wash it there. And then there was a Serb who I called Glavonja and he brought it. And once I think the warden himself brought it and left it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Yugo car, what kind of a car is it? Does it have a particular brand?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It's actually a Zastava vehicle. One was called a Yugo 45, another one was called a Yugo 55 and then there was a Zastava 101. But at any rate, it was Zastava made.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that it was the warden's car?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't know how come I know, but I know that I saw him driving it often and I know that this Glavonja who brought me the car, he told "Lija, clean the warden's car now." I don't know whether it was his car. I mean, that was the impression I had. It's not that I have any documentation. He personally, Glavonja said to me -- once I also think that the warden, Krnojelac, came there and left it there, because I saw him in it often.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This Serb, Glavonja, was he a staff member?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. He was a worker at the KP Dom. He issued fuel to drivers for trucks of the KP Dom. So I would go and help him pour the fuel also into this Yugo with a pump. Glavonja was my nickname for him, but I never knew in my life what his name and surname were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How often did you actually service the warden's car?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, it would happen that for some reason, on some days, when no one worked, they would take me out and give me this car and I would clean it for a long, long time, because it was nicer for me than to sit up in the room. I could pinch something, steal something, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What would you steal?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: It had to do with tobacco, tobacco, cigarettes. Sorry. I didn't mean steal. I mean, they would leave me on my own, so I would have the chance of looking around and taking some tobacco from some room. I mean, it all had to do with tobacco.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you continue to see this car or service this car after Mr. Krnojelac was replaced by a new warden?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I think I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Besides the workshop, did you work in other areas within the KP Dom? You have already mentioned that you had some work to do in the isolation cell. Where else did you work within the KP Dom compound?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I worked all over the KP Dom, in all the rooms at the KP Dom where there were any pipes or water pipes. I worked everywhere, in all of those places. From the roof down, including entrance doors, offices. I think I worked in 95 per cent of all the premises of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever work in the warden's office?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where was it within the building? On which floor was it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: What do you mean, in the building?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the administration building, on which floor was the warden's office?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, let me see how many floors there were. I think it was the second floor. It was along the corridor. You go straight, then you go upstairs, then you go through the back door into that building. I think there are no more offices or doors after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I would like to show the witness Exhibit 6/3. It's a plan of the second floor of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you point -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at the warden's office, the room that --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: This is the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The room next to the entrance to the KP Dom, right-hand side. Yes. Thank you. In which period -- thank you. In which period did you work in this room? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Due to that wartime system, the KP Dom building was heated through the steam aggregate, steam pipeline, and they provided heating for themselves in the winter. It was end 1992, beginning of 1993 I had to clean the chimneys because they were dirty, and I had to install a furnace into that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The KP Dom, did it not have a central heating system? You had pointed out to us previously the boiler room.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think you didn't quite understand me. I said that when the boiler room stopped working, because it was broken, and in 1992 it wasn't operational. It used to work before. And the chimneys, which I cleaned, hadn't been cleaned for 20 years, because the steam pipe hadn't worked for the previous 20 years. It wasn't working at the moment, in December, and before that it was in operation; it was being used.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how, then, was the administration building kept warm at that time when you worked there? What did they use? I didn't really understand the system. Did they have stoves in each room or how was it kept warm?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Maybe I can make it clearer like this: In 1990, 1991, and 1992, there was a central heating. In end 1992, there was no central heating, because the system, the heating system, was broken, because the boiler room was not operational; it was broken. So they used firewood and coal. And I had to clean out the chimneys, which hadn't worked for ages, and they put furnaces into their offices to keep warm.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about the prisoners' rooms? Did you have to prepare them as well? Did you put stoves in there and clean the chimneys?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Let me see. I think in 1993 and 1994 we had heating, while in 1992, December 1992, and then January 1993, we didn't have any heating, so we had heating after October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In 1992, when you made these furnaces for the administration building, could you have as well made furnaces for the prisoners' rooms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't think we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: How do I know? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was material available? Could you have done that if you were ordered to do so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I did that in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you have done that in 1992 as well if someone had ordered you to do so?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, if I did it in 1993, why couldn't I have done it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you worked in Mr. Krnojelac's office. Was he ever in the office when you worked there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He stood there once. He was looking for something in his -- on his shelf. And then I was working in the room next to his. He was there in the room, but not all the time.
