He would leave occasionally. And while we were doing our jobs in those offices, not only the warden's office, but also the ones next door, they moved around. They would come and go. He stood there for a while, then he went elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever see lists related to detainees on his desk?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I didn't see any about prisoners, but I once saw a paper with my name on it on the desk. I couldn't see much really. While I was standing there I just peeked at it. I could see my name. It was the fourth from the top on a list. It was just lying on the table like this sheet is now lying here. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many names were on this sheet of paper? Do you recall? You said yours was the fourth name.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to make any conclusions now. I didn't count then. I didn't read much, because I didn't dare. I just glanced at it. And in my estimate, there were about ten, a dozen names, judging by the number of lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you present when this sheet of paper with the names on it was actually given to Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You mean that paper specifically?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think once, and I think it was on that occasion precisely, Savo Todovic and Krnojelac were both there sitting in adjacent offices, and they were moving around, coming and going. They were handing those papers, and it's difficult it say definitively whether it was this paper or not. I can hardly say with any certainty. I came here to tell the truth and I'm afraid to tale lie if I venture a guess. Maybe it was that paper, maybe it wasn't. Because he had lots of those on his desk. They were just lying around.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you hear any conversation between Mr. Todovic and Mr. Krnojelac in relation to papers on the desk or that Mr. Todovic had?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I cannot recall at the moment that I had any conversation related to that. Maybe I did hear it, but I cannot recall now. I don't think I did, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you worked outside the KP Dom compound, did you ever see bodies in the Drina River in front of the KP Dom-? Do you recall anything?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, once. I went there with this Arso, Krnojelac's brother. He was with me. I was pushing this machine. I think Zeka and I were together. That is outside the KP Dom, on the road towards the hospital. There were some old vehicles and trailers there on that lot we were supposed to take some parts of for our purposes. And while we were going there, there is like an island or something, and I saw some clothes floating. And Zeko told me just before, "Look at those corpses over there." And I looked and I saw a body indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But you did not recognise who it was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No way. I couldn't know. I didn't come close. It was at a distance of about 10, 15 metres from the place where I was standing and where I was doing my job. You could see it was a corpse, but you couldn't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you see that? Which year was it, and which month, if you can say?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: All of that was somewhere in the period from early July to the 15th of August, or perhaps the beginning of July, the beginning of August. I think it was in July. I want you to know when you're asking questions like this, I've told you this already: Years 1992 and 1993 blended in my mind into one year, and I cannot say, otherwise very roughly, when things happened. It could have been June, it could have been July, but it's certainly not May and it's not September either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "June," "July," is that 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to read something. Do you recall that you gave a statement to the Prosecutor's office in 1999? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, please. Go ahead. I hope I'll remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will now read from page 9, paragraph 3 of the document number 318/A of the trial binders, and in the B/C/S version it's also page 9 and it is paragraph 4 -- no, not 4. This one. Five. It's paragraph 5. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "On one occasion in either October or November, 1992, I had to clean the steam heating in Krnojelac's office. Ekrem Zekovic or Maljanovic or the worker Berberkic were working with me. I'm not sure who of the three were working with me on this occasion. While we were working in Krnojelac's office, Todovic came in with a list. He presented the list to Krnojelac and said that the detainees on this list should be taken out. Krnojelac looked at the list, obviously checking and considering. Because we left the room immediately after this, we could not hear if Krnojelac approved the taking." Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Could you repeat this, please, once again?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "On one occasion in either October or November" -- would it help you to read it yourself? I can also put the document in front of you so that you can read this paragraph yourself. Would it help you more?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: You can read it to me. I'll listen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "On one occasion in either October or November 1992, I had to clean the steam heating in Krnojelac's office. Ekrem Zekovic or Maljanovic or the worker Berberkic were working with me. I'm not sure who of the three were working with me on this occasion. While we were working in Krnojelac's office, Todovic came in with a list. He presented the list to Krnojelac and said that the detainees on this list should be taken out. Krnojelac looked at the list, obviously checking and considering. Because we left immediately after this, we could not hear if Krnojelac approved the taking."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I'd like to have it in front of me and read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness has been given page 9 in the B/C/S version, and the paragraph is indicated to him by just a little mark.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: What's written here, on one occasion in either October or November 1992, I had to clean the steam heating in Krnojelac's office," that's not true, because I was cleaning the chimneys. Well, it says here, "Berberkic," I'm not sure who of the three were working with me on this occasion. I would correct this. I think I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. don't know that I ever gave this statement. I know that Savo Todovic had papers all the time and that he was handing them over to Krnojelac, but I don't know about this for prisoners, that prisoners should be taken out. Maybe I did say this, but I would like to correct this part. Maybe it was a misunderstanding due to interpretation or I used a different expression, I put it differently. I don't know. It's true that he had a look at the list, because Savo Todovic carried his bag like this, under his arm, and he contacted with Krnojelac all the time and he would hand him papers. That much is true. But I don't know about what's written here. "He presented the list to Krnojelac and said that the detainees on the list should be taken ..." First of all, I would never use the word "detainee." I would have said Muslims or inmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I cannot tell you about this, but I don't think this is my statement. Maybe it was a misunderstanding. I think it was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. It's clarified now. Thank you. In relation to the work that you did, was it hard work, physically hard work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: The work that I did was my job even before the war. It was metalworking. It's a difficult job, for a myriad of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you -- after work, when you returned to your room, were you exhausted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: That depends. Sometimes. I was always exhausted. All of us were. I was exhausted all the time, but sometimes more, sometimes less. If, for instance, I would go to the hospital and get more food, I was less exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did other detainees have to work on the front lines? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I personally didn't see them, but some people told me that they had been close to the front lines, that they gathered hay for the farm, that they drove trucks. But I personally didn't see them doing that, because I hadn't been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know a Mujo Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had to work? Do you know if he had to work on the front line?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, listen. I don't want to get this mixed up. There is one Mujo Hodzic and there is another Hodzic as well. One of them worked with the people who gathered hay and the other one was a house painter, and he worked with me in the same shop. The one who gathered hay, Mujo Hodzic -- the Mujo Hodzic that I knew didn't work. I don't know. Maybe you can look it up in my statement. There are also people with the last name of Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know if any detainees had to work on the front lines digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Oh, good. Good. I know what you're asking now. About this Mujo Hodzic, precisely. I've just remembered. This man was taken away, and it was not only him; it was a group of about 15 or 20. They were taken away, I don't know where, but it was approximately in the autumn. I think two months later, the same people were returned to the KP Dom and we were very surprised to see them back. I spoke personally to that Mujo Hodzic. What they told me was that they had been somewhere at the front line digging some trenches, sleeping in barracks with Serbs, with soldiers, and then they were returned to the KP Dom. If that is what you mean, I know about it, but that's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said in autumn. Is that 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think it was autumn 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to discuss schedule E with the witness. It should be in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we do not need to talk about all these people that you see on schedule E. Just the ones that I will refer you to. The person number 1, Uzeir Aganovic, did he work in the metalwork shop together with you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When? Do you recall at what period he worked?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He worked there in 1992 and in 1993. He was there all the time. If that is the Aganovic, Uzeir I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The person listed under number 5, Muharem Bacvic, Bacvic, yes, did he work in the KP Dom, and in which field of work did he work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I know one Bacvic who didn't work at all. But wait a minute. This Bacvic, Muharem, I can't remember now. Bacvic, Muharem. Bacvic, Muharem, Bacvic, Muharem. I think he worked at the carpentry shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 10, the worker Berberkic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Berberkic was a tin Smith. He worked together with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 13, Izet Causevic [sic], where did he work, if he worked?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Izet Cosovic or Causevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Cosovic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know according to name -- oh, I know. Here. Fine. Great. It says so. He worked -- he was a jack of all trades. He did not have a specific job.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Number 16 on the next page, number 16, Enver Cemo, where did he work, if he worked?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He was also a jack of all trades. He worked at the farm and in the compound, different things.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Number 17, Mujo Dudic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: For some time, that was the main cleaning lady of the administration building, for one period of time. And then after that he worked up at the farm. But I think he spent most of the time around the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 18?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He was there briefly. He was taken somewhere later. Actually, I have his brother in mind. His brother. He also worked a bit around the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 20?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, there were two Gogalijas there. Gogalija, Asim and another Gogalija. One of the Gogalijas work at the carpentry and then he was taken somewhere, and the other one was released. Now, I don't know who is Asim and who is Kasim. I don't know which is the one referred to here. One of them worked at the carpentry, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Number 25, Munib Hadzic, did he work, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He worked with me, together with me at the metalwork shop. He was one of the first people in the metalwork shop where I was. He went somewhere after that. I said goodbye to him on the bus. The bus was parked. And he went somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What does that mean, he went somewhere? Does that mean he disappeared or was he released?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He went for an exchange. That was a successful exchange, because I know that he's alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 28, Murid Islambasic, did he work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Murid Islambasic? If I'm referring to the baker/driver, he went somewhere in the morning and then they would return him in the evening. I don't know where he went, whether he went for an interrogation or to work somewhere. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he kept separate from other detainees or ...

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, was he isolated then? At that time there were perhaps 500 or 600 detainees, and I was out there. I went to work and then I came back in the afternoon. I mean, well, possibly he was separate. Perhaps he was in one of the rooms. I think perhaps he was separate. I have no idea. At any rate, he was not present in any one of the rooms that I knew, that I knew about. And then, you know, there were lots of rooms there, from 11 to Room 20. There are 10 or 15 rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 29, did this person, Suad Islambasic, did he have to work?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: When Munib and Suad Islambasic worked -- actually, this Munib Hodzic worked with me and Suad Islambasic. He worked -- actually, he worked before Mr. -- Mr. -- Mr. -- Mr. -- Mr. -- the one who has a code-name 249.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. So he worked in the metalwork shop, this Mr. Suad --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. At the mechanic's department. He was a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 30, Atif Jasarevic, did he have to work, and where?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: He also did all sorts of things. He went out with the grass cutters and he did work related to the farm. When I'm talking about the farm, I'm referring to the farm that had to do with agriculture, so I'm talking about agriculture, cutting grass, collecting hay, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Number 31, Karahasanovic, do you know this person, and did he have to work, and what?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: At the same time, if you mean Karahasanovic, the forwarder, because there were lots of them at the camp, if you mean the one nickname Karasi, then he worked with me together. I think it was him. I don't think it was someone else. He worked with me and sometimes he would help me and sometimes he would help the mechanics. Then You keep asking me whether we had to all the time. I think we've taken care of that, whether we had to or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Number 33, did he work, Saban Karup?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Saban Karup, yes. He used to drive an FAP truck that belonged to the KP Dom, a yellow one. He also worked together with Jasarevic up there. So they were actually collecting the crops for cattle feed.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Krkalic, Rasim. Rasim Krkalic. I'm a bit confused right now. I simply do not have his image before my eyes now. I know him well, but right now I just can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. We can move on. 38, Goran Kukavica, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I think he never did anything while he was here at the KP Dom Foca. I saw him once in Sarajevo. Perhaps that's not important. I don't think he did anything in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 42, Maljanovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: 42, Maljanovic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Fine. There were two Maljanovics. One worked with me all the time and the other one from time to time, so I don't know which one you're referring to. These are actually two half brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If you look at 43, you see Ramiz or Asim. Would that be the first names of the brothers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Great. Yes. Yes. Asim. Asim is the one who worked with me all the time, and Maljanovic worked from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 44, Sacir Muratovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: A tailor. A tailor at the carpentry shop. He cut fabrics for upholstery.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 49?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Reko Taib. He was with the grass cutters. He had to do with the farm and with cutting grass and collecting hay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 50?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Sahovic, Ifet. Right now I've lost his image too. I can't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And 51?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Saraka Ramiz. Well, he was not in Foca for a long time. He worked in the compound. I think he left early. I don't know when he left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say he worked in the compound, do you mean within the yard of the main prison or where?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to the main yard. Because they had to clean the yard itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And number 52, Dzevad Sosevic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Sosevic, Dzevad. He worked for a while with the hay cutters, the grass cutters, and those who were collecting hay. This had to do with the farm, Brioni. And he also went before others did; at least, that is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And at last, 57 and 58, the two tailors, did they work, and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Telo, Aziz and Telo, Mustafa. Yes. I think they were the main people there, from the beginning to the end. They worked at Brioni, at the farm there, and they had to do with cutting grass and collecting hay for the cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say they worked there from the beginning to the end, does that mean they worked there as long as you did, that is, until October 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We are finished with this part. Witness, while you were at the KP Dom, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: When Zeka escaped.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At that time when this happened, was Mr. Krnojelac still the warden, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't know, but at any rate he was in the building. You know what, when you say "warden," I don't know who appointed who where, but he was there. He was there, he was in the building. And when Zeka escaped, he was in the building, as he was in 1992. He was there then too. Now, whether he was the warden, whether he was the director, what he was, I don't know. He was some kind of an important person, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Zekovic actually wanted to escape before he did it actually?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, because I was preparing an escape together with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did you and he -- and Mr. Zekovic, why did you want to escape at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Why? Why I wanted to escape? Well, everybody who is in prison tries to escape if he has a chance. So I was in a camp. I mean, it was my wish to escape, because of the pressure, because of the conditions, the living conditions I had there. It's hard to explain this directly right now. Ask anybody who was in a camp, in a prison, whether he wanted to escape if he had a chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was it noticed that Mr. Zekovic was missing, and who actually noticed that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I noticed it because I knew that he would escape, but I didn't know when. Because I had given up. And then I thought that he might too, but as soon as I saw that he was missing I realised that he had escaped. We noticed it some time around 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did the guards notice?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Some of us -- I mean, there were 7 or 10 of us there at that moment - while we were having dinner, or no, rather, lunch, I said to one of them, "Did you know that Zeka is missing?" And then one of them got really scared and he went directly to one of the guards and told him that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To whom did you say, "Did you know that Zeka is missing?" Did you say that to a detainee or to a guard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Detainee. A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened after the guard was informed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: What happened? A state of alert, emergency. They returned us to the other place, to the metalwork shop, where he worked. We didn't go back to the rooms. And of course, all these provocations started: "Where is Zeka?" They pressured me most of all: "You were friends with him. Where is he? Where? Where? Tell us, where is he?" So these provocations. I don't know what you are really interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I want you to tell us what happened on that day after he left, Mr. Zekovic escaped. You said you were taken to the metal shop. Who from the prison staff was present in the metal shop?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Everybody was present, everybody, all of those who worked at the KP Dom. I can't say with 100 per cent certainty, but those who were on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the shift and those who were not on the shift were present. I would say that it was some kind of mobilisation. I mean, everybody was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was Mr. Krnojelac present?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I saw him there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were you beaten while you were in the -- while you were questioned in the metal shop?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes. Pljevaljcic slapped me in the face and he dragged me out there to walk. I always said that perhaps the man fell asleep and did not hear the time He slapped me in the face and then this mistreatment started. And then I was walking through this metal shop from one room to another. We were allegedly looking for him. Not allegedly. I was looking for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From the metalwork shop, where were you taken next?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: They returned us to this hall that I explained a few minutes ago, where that reception room is and that hall that enters the KP Dom, and also this hall that links up the administration building and the KP Dom. How should I call it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the photo 7446, this one, and 7470, this one, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you look at this photo, is that part of the hall that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This part here. There should be another photograph here, because there is another hall here. Yes, this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing on the floor in front of this kind of reception desk. And can we have the other photo, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It's this part here, precisely this part here, because this part has to do with the first part that I showed you. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mean these two parts are connected?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I don't think; I know. The door was always open.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has pointed at the room shown in 7470.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And when you were there, what happened in this hall? First of all, who was in the hall? Who of the detainees and who of the staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: All of us who were at the metalwork shop were there, and there were also lots of guards who were going left and right, up and down, all over the place. They were milling about. And then beating started, and a lot of them were yelling and saying, "Tell us, where is Zeka? We're going to kill you." So they threatened us and they beat us. That moment they took me to this reception office - you haven't got that picture here - and Savo Todovic took me there directly, and Boro Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, we do not have a photo of this room that you just mentioned, but I would like to show you the floor plan. It's the floor plan, the Exhibit 6/1. Can you point out the room where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: This is the hall, this is the reception desk, then this is the room here, here, where there is this interrupted thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness was pointing at the room -- the next room left to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And you said that -- you said that Mr. Todovic and - let me just see - Mr. Todovic and Mr. Ivanovic, Boro Ivanovic, took you there, and what did they do there when you were there with him? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, I'll be repeating things again. At the same time, the same questions - where is Zeka? Where did he go? In which directions? What are his intentions? - that I should tell them about all of that because I knew about it. They threatened me. They walked up real close to me. Boro walked up to me to hit me on the head with a pistol. He did not hit me, though. That kind of thing. So all the time the same story was being repeated: Where was he, and also these provocative questions, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they beat you? You said that Mr. Boro Ivanovic threatened you and he even tried as if he wanted to hit you. Were you actually beaten by the two of them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: No. Boro approached me with a pistol. Savo was standing on the side, and then he said - I have to tell you this literally - that he would hang me by the balls and that he would skin me like a goat. And then he came forward with a gun, but he did not hit me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And before, when you were still together with the other members of the workshop, of the work group, in this main hall, did you see who was beaten by whom? Did you notice?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: Well, listen. They took me out of that room a hundred times and then they returned me to the isolation cell and then to that hall, and then we went to the building where these isolation cells were. They were beating people. They were beating people. Now, who beat whom, personally -- I mean, I was beaten by Pljevaljcic and another one. I can't remember his name. Who else was there? I know that Maric slapped someone in the face there, but, you know, I was looking ahead and there was lots of panic, and you could not really look around and see who was beating whom. Everybody was beaten, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr Rasevic beat anyone?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see what Mr. Krnojelac did?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED LISICA
utterances.text: I saw him moving around there. He was there. He would dart in, dart out. How can I put this to you? He looked as if the KP Dom was on fire and that now the fire was being extinguished, and the Muslims were the victims. Something like that. I didn't see him personally beating anyone. Maybe he did beat someone, but I don't know.
